query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, atomic layer deposited alumina coating to a MoNbTaW‐based refractory high‐entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance by directly seeding the formation of a continuous and protective alumina scale.
generation.material_initial_state: MoNbTaW‐based refractory high‐entropy alloy that, in its untreated state, rapidly oxidizes at high temperatures due to the inability to form a robust protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Application of a high-temperature–stable, thin alumina coating using atomic layer deposition.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1100–1200°C in an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air) for durations on the order of 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The pre-formed alumina layer acts as a seed, enabling the development and stabilization of a continuous alumina (Al2O3) scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The thin alumina coating acts as a diffusion barrier that limits the ingress of oxygen and the outward diffusion of reactive metal elements. This controlled surface modification stabilizes the growth of a protective alumina oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, thus retarding further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the alumina-coated alloy will exhibit a much lower weight gain due to reduced oxidation, a thinner yet more continuous oxide scale, and better retention of mechanical properties under high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy forms non-protective oxide scales that allow rapid oxidation and degradation during high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The benefit of the coating may be compromised if the coating adheres poorly, degrades (e.g., spallation) during thermal cycling, or if the coating processing introduces defects. The hypothesis is limited to conditions where the coating integrity is maintained over the exposure period.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of oxidation improvement is not defined and may vary with coating thickness, deposition quality, and exact service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MoNbTaW-based refractory high-entropy alloy samples. Using atomic layer deposition, apply a thin alumina coating on one set while leaving the other set uncoated. Expose both sets to an air atmosphere at approximately 1150°C for 100 hours.
measurements: Thermogravimetric analysis to monitor weight gain over time
Surface characterization using X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy to assess oxide scale composition and integrity
Mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation or tensile testing) to evaluate retention of structural properties after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alumina-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in weight gain, exhibit a less continuous/protective oxide scale, or do not retain improved mechanical properties compared to uncoated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The maximum temperature of useful resistance to oxidation with different oxide barriers can be estimated from the parabolic rate constants. A useful limit for materials in thin sections is kP ≈ 10−10 g2·cm−4·s−1 (weight gain 6 mg·cm−2 in 100 h). At this limit, alloys that form chromia as a scale would be useful to 1100 °C (close to the upper limit for Cr base alloys and (high Cr) Ni or Co base alloys). Alumina and silica formers would be useful respectively to 1425 °C and 1750 °C []. The maximum useful temperature for Nb-silicide based alloys, the oxidation resistance of which cannot rely on chromia scales, is determined by the melting point of Nb2O5 based mixed oxides (see below). In the case of refractory metal intermetallic based alloys, like Nb or Mo silicide based alloys, another important requirement is that the accelerated catastrophic oxidation, known as pest oxidation, that occurs at low temperatures is eliminated []. Suppression of pest oxidation in Mo and Nb silicide based alloys is possible via the synergy of specific alloying additions, which control the vol % of the solid solution and lead to stabilisation of specific phases in the alloy microstructure. Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
